papers.name: Paper 1: Explorations in creative reading and writing
papers.covers: Section A, 40 marks, reads one prose fiction extract from the 20th or 21st century, printed in a separate insert: Question 1, list four things from a few given lines (4 marks, AO1); Question 2, how the writer uses language in a given passage (8 marks, AO2); Question 3, how the writer has structured the whole text (8 marks, AO2); Question 4, how far you agree with a student's statement about part of the text (20 marks, AO4). Section B, 40 marks, is one piece of creative writing from a choice of two, a description suggested by a picture or a story from a prompt, related to the topic of the extract: 24 marks for content and organisation (AO5) and 16 for technical accuracy (AO6). The paper advises about 15 minutes reading, 45 on Section A and 45 on Section B. In June 2024 the extract was from Doris Lessing's The Grass is Singing, and the writing choice was a description of a very hot place or a story about a disagreement. Half of the GCSE.

papers.name: Paper 2: Writers' viewpoints and perspectives
papers.covers: Section A, 40 marks, reads two linked non-fiction texts, one from the 19th century and one from the 20th or 21st, printed in an insert: Question 1, choose four true statements from eight about a few lines of Source A (4 marks, AO1); Question 2, a summary of what you understand from both sources on a given point (8 marks, AO1); Question 3, how the writer uses language in a passage of one source (12 marks, AO2); Question 4, compare how the two writers convey their different feelings and perspectives (16 marks, AO3). Section B, 40 marks, is one piece of writing that presents a viewpoint on a statement, in a named form for a named audience, such as an article for a school magazine, a letter or a speech: 24 marks for content and organisation (AO5) and 16 for technical accuracy (AO6). In June 2024 the sources were Adam Kay's diary of a junior doctor (2017) and Mary Seacole's memoir (1857), and the writing task was an article arguing a point of view on choosing a career. Half of the GCSE. The Spoken Language endorsement, a formal presentation with questions assessed by the teacher on AO7 to AO9, is reported separately as Pass, Merit or Distinction and carries no marks towards the grade.

commandWords.word: List four things about … from this part of the source
commandWords.meaning: Paper 1 Question 1. Four separate points, each from the given lines only, each true, each about the named subject. A quotation or a paraphrase both count and a single word can be enough; a point from outside the lines, or a point about the setting when the question asks about a character, earns nothing.

commandWords.word: How does the writer use language here to …
commandWords.meaning: Paper 1 Question 2, which prints three bullets, and Paper 2 Question 3, which prints none and drops the word here. Only the given lines. The Paper 1 bullets name the ground: words and phrases, language features and techniques, sentence forms. The top level analyses the effects of the writer's choices with judicious detail and sophisticated terminology; naming a technique without its effect stays in the lower levels.

commandWords.word: How has the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader?
commandWords.meaning: Paper 1 Question 3. The whole source. Structure means what the writer focuses on first, how and why the focus moves, and any other structural feature: shifts of time, place or perspective, a widening or narrowing of view, dialogue, an ending that answers the opening. A response that writes only about language is answering Question 2's objective and earns little here.

commandWords.word: To what extent do you agree?
commandWords.meaning: Paper 1 Question 4, twenty marks. A student's statement about part of the source is given; the answer takes a position on it, evaluates how the writer's methods create the impression, and supports every point with the text. The top level develops a convincing and critical response to the focus of the statement, with perceptive understanding of methods.

commandWords.word: Choose four statements below which are true
commandWords.meaning: Paper 2 Question 1. Eight statements about a few lines of Source A, exactly four of them true. The instructions say to choose a maximum of four. Read the lines again before deciding, because the false statements are built from words that are in the passage.

commandWords.word: Use details from both sources to write a summary of …
commandWords.meaning: Paper 2 Question 2, eight marks, AO1. A summary of what you understand about the given point from both texts, with a detail from each. Interpretation earns more than listing: the top level makes perceptive inferences from both texts and synthesises evidence. No analysis of language is wanted here.

commandWords.word: Compare how the writers convey their different feelings and perspectives on …
commandWords.meaning: Paper 2 Question 4, sixteen marks, AO3. Both whole sources. Compare the perspectives, compare the methods used to convey them, and support with references to both texts. The top level compares ideas and perspectives in a perceptive way and analyses how methods convey them; writing about one text at a time is not a comparison.

commandWords.word: Write a description … as suggested by this picture / Write a story about …
commandWords.meaning: Paper 1 Question 5, forty marks. One choice of two. The picture is a starting point, not a thing to be described in order; the story prompt is a subject, not a title. Twenty-four marks for content and organisation reward convincing communication, ambitious vocabulary, crafted devices and structural features used with intent; sixteen for technical accuracy reward secure sentences, a wide range of punctuation and accurate spelling.

commandWords.word: Write an article / a letter / a speech in which you argue / explain / persuade …
commandWords.meaning: Paper 2 Question 5, forty marks. The statement gives the issue, the task gives the form and the audience. The form's conventions are expected, a headline and standfirst for an article, a greeting and sign-off for a letter, address to the room for a speech, and the tone, style and register must match purpose and audience assuredly for the top level.

assessmentObjectives.meaning: Identify and interpret explicit and implicit information and ideas; select and synthesise evidence from different texts. Paper 1 Question 1 (4 marks) and Paper 2 Questions 1 and 2 (4 and 8 marks).

Explain, comment on and analyse how writers use language and structure to achieve effects and influence readers, using relevant subject terminology to support views. Paper 1 Questions 2 and 3 (8 marks each) and Paper 2 Question 3 (12 marks).
Compare writers' ideas and perspectives, as well as how these are conveyed, across two or more texts. Paper 2 Question 4 (16 marks) only.
Evaluate texts critically and support this with appropriate textual references. Paper 1 Question 4 (20 marks) only.

Communicate clearly, effectively and imaginatively, selecting and adapting tone, style and register for different forms, purposes and audiences; organise information and ideas, using structural and grammatical features to support coherence and cohesion. Twenty-four of the forty writing marks on each paper, for content and organisation.

Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation. Sixteen of the forty writing marks on each paper, for technical accuracy; the specification requires this to be 20% of the whole qualification.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Language analysis: Paper 1 Question 2 (8 marks) and Paper 2 Question 3 (12 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: Stays inside the given lines, chooses two or three details worth the time rather than the first ones found, and for each names the choice, the effect and the reason the effect follows from the words, moving from a single word to an image to a sentence form. Terminology is exact and used to explain, not to decorate. The June 2024 Level 4 example analysed one image and one simile and the verb inside them, and that was enough.

Reads the whole source as a shape: what the writer puts first and why, where the focus moves and what the move does, how time passes, whose perspective the reader shares, and how the ending sits against the opening. Names structural features rather than language features, and explains the effect of each on the reader's interest. The mark scheme lists exposition, focus shifts, narrative perspective, temporal shifts, flashback, dialogue and anti-climax as the kind of thing it rewards.

Takes the statement apart into its claims, decides how far each holds, and argues it with the writer's methods: this simile presents her as trapped, this shift of perspective at the end hands her the power. Agrees and disagrees where the text supports each, and says so. Every judgement has a quotation under it and every quotation has a method named.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Summary and comparison: Paper 2 Questions 2 and 4 (8 and 16 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: For the summary, inferences from both texts drawn together on the given point, not two lists. For the comparison, both writers' perspectives stated and set against each other, then the methods by which each conveys a perspective compared, with references from both texts in every paragraph, and a sense of how the two periods shape the two views.

A plan with a shape before the first sentence: an opening that places the reader, a movement of focus or time, and an ending that returns to something planted earlier. Vocabulary chosen for precision rather than size, devices used where they do something, sentence forms varied for effect, paragraphs that connect. Then five minutes of checking, because sixteen marks are for accuracy and a wide range of punctuation used well.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Writing to present a viewpoint: Paper 2 Question 5 (40 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: A clear position on the statement, held throughout, with the form's conventions in place and the audience addressed as the task names it. Ideas developed, not listed; a counter-argument met; a tone that suits the form, whether the wit of an article or the address of a speech. Discourse markers integrated rather than bolted on, and the same care over accuracy as on Paper 1.
